resources.title: Housing — Brussels
resources.body: Brussels has a competitive rental market; most long-term rentals are unfurnished and require a written lease registered with the regional authority. Furnished flats in central communes (Ixelles, Saint-Gilles, City of Brussels) carry a premium. A rental guarantee (deposit) is typically placed in a blocked bank account in the tenant's name.

resources.title: Banking — Brussels
resources.body: Opening a resident current account generally requires proof of identity, proof of a Brussels address, and a National Register number (or proof of registration in progress). Some banks open a limited 'basic bank account' before full registration is complete.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Brussels
resources.body: Brussels schooling is split between the French Community and Flemish Community networks, alongside a large international and European school sector serving expatriate families. Enrolment in local schools runs through community-specific registration procedures.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Brussels
resources.body: New residents must register at their local commune (commune/gemeente) of residence, which triggers an address verification by the local police and entry in the National Register. Registration is the gateway to most administrative services, including obtaining a residence card.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Brussels
resources.body: Belgian residents are identified for tax and administrative purposes by their National Register number, issued on registration at the commune. Residents file annual personal income tax with the federal tax administration; employment income is taxed via payroll withholding.

resources.title: Transport — Brussels
resources.body: Brussels public transport (metro, tram, bus) is operated by STIB-MIVB, with regional and national rail complementing it. Monthly and annual travel passes are available on a rechargeable card. New residents from outside the EU/EEA may need to exchange their driving licence via their commune.

resources.title: Housing — Berlin
resources.body: Berlin's rental market is highly competitive and tenant-protective. Most flats are unfurnished (often without kitchen/appliances) and let long-term. Newcomers typically need Schufa credit report, proof of income, and prior-landlord reference. Cold rent (Kaltmiete) excludes utilities; warm rent (Warmmiete) includes them. A rent cap (Mietspiegel) benchmarks legal rents. Expect strong demand in central districts (Mitte, Prenzlauer Berg, Kreuzberg, Charlottenburg).

resources.title: Banking — Berlin
resources.body: Opening a current account (Girokonto) requires proof of address (registration/Anmeldung), passport/ID, and often the tax ID. Both traditional banks and app-based providers operate widely; many expats use digital banks for fast English-language onboarding. A local IBAN is essential for rent, salary and SEPA direct debits.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Berlin
resources.body: Berlin offers free public (state) schools taught in German, plus a large selection of bilingual, international, and private schools for expat families. International schools follow foreign or dual curricula and charge tuition; demand is high and waitlists common. School attendance is compulsory from age six.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Berlin
resources.body: After arriving and securing housing, residents must register their address in person. Non-EU nationals additionally need a residence/work permit from the immigration office. Registration triggers issuance of the tax ID and is prerequisite for banking, health insurance and many services. Appointments are often required and can book out weeks ahead.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Berlin
resources.body: Germany assigns a lifelong tax ID automatically after address registration, mailed by the federal tax office. Employees are taxed via payroll (Lohnsteuer) with progressive rates plus solidarity surcharge and, if applicable, church tax. Tax class (Steuerklasse) affects withholding; annual returns are filed with the local tax office (Finanzamt).

resources.title: Transport — Berlin
resources.body: Berlin has an extensive integrated public transport network covering U-Bahn (metro), S-Bahn (suburban rail), trams, buses and ferries across fare zones A/B/C. Tickets and monthly passes work across all modes. Cycling infrastructure is strong. A nationwide monthly ticket (Deutschlandticket) is also widely used.

resources.title: Housing — Frankfurt
resources.body: Frankfurt has one of Germany's tightest and most expensive rental markets, driven by its banking sector. Apartments are typically unfurnished (often without kitchens/light fixtures). Tenants usually pay a deposit (Kaution) of up to three months' cold rent held in a separate account, and many rentals require a Schufa credit report and proof of income. A Schufa-based letting agent commission may apply, though since 2015 the Bestellerprinzip means the party who hires the agent pays the fee.

resources.title: Banking — Frankfurt
resources.body: Opening a German bank account (Girokonto) generally requires a passport/ID, proof of registered address (Meldebescheinigung from the Bürgeramt), and often a residence permit and proof of income or employment. Both traditional branch banks and app-based banks operate; SEPA transfers and the Girocard debit system are standard.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Frankfurt
resources.body: Frankfurt hosts a large international community and a wide range of international schools offering IB, British, American, French and other curricula, alongside German state schools (Grundschule, Gymnasium). Placement in international schools is competitive and fee-paying; state schooling is free but taught in German.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Frankfurt
resources.body: Newcomers must register their residence (Anmeldung) at a local Bürgeramt within roughly two weeks of moving in, presenting a passport, rental contract and a landlord confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung). Registration produces a Meldebescheinigung needed for banking, tax and other services. Non-EU nationals additionally need a residence permit from the Ausländerbehörde.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Frankfurt
resources.body: After registration, residents are issued a tax identification number (Steuer-Identifikationsnummer / Steuer-ID) by post, required for employment and payroll. Income tax is withheld at source via wage tax (Lohnsteuer) based on tax classes (Steuerklassen); annual tax returns are filed with the Finanzamt.

resources.title: Transport — Frankfurt
resources.body: Frankfurt has an extensive integrated public transport network of U-Bahn, S-Bahn, trams and buses coordinated within the RMV regional tariff association. Monthly tickets are available, and the nationwide Deutschlandticket offers unlimited regional/local travel. Healthcare requires enrolment in statutory (gesetzliche) or private health insurance, mandatory for residents and usually arranged via the employer.

resources.title: Housing — Hamburg
resources.body: Hamburg's rental market is competitive and tight, especially in central districts (Mitte, Eimsbüttel, Altona). Furnished and unfurnished flats are typically found via online portals; expect strong demand, required proof of income, and a SCHUFA credit report. Cold rent (Kaltmiete) excludes utilities (Nebenkosten).

resources.title: Banking — Hamburg
resources.body: Opening a German bank account (Girokonto) generally requires proof of identity, proof of address (often the Anmeldung registration confirmation), and sometimes proof of income or residence permit. Traditional banks and app-based banks both serve newcomers.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Hamburg
resources.body: Hamburg offers public (state) schools free of charge as well as international and bilingual schools serving expatriate families. International schools follow various curricula and typically charge tuition; state schools teach in German.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Hamburg
resources.body: New residents must register their address (Anmeldung) at a local citizen's office (Bürgeramt/Kundenzentrum) shortly after moving in, presenting a passport and a landlord confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung). This registration is a prerequisite for most other administrative steps.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Hamburg
resources.body: After registering, residents are issued a tax identification number by the federal tax authority, used for payroll and tax purposes. Income tax is withheld via the employer under the wage tax (Lohnsteuer) system, and tax classes affect withholding.

resources.title: Transport — Hamburg
resources.body: Hamburg has an extensive integrated public transport network of U-Bahn, S-Bahn, buses and ferries operated within a single tariff association. The nationwide Deutschlandticket provides unlimited regional/local travel for a flat monthly fee. Newcomers must also arrange health insurance, which is mandatory in Germany.

resources.title: Housing — Munich
resources.body: Munich is Germany's most expensive rental market. Furnished and unfurnished flats in central districts are scarce and competitive; expect to provide proof of income (Gehaltsnachweise), a SCHUFA credit report and a landlord reference (Mietschuldenfreiheitsbescheinigung). Deposits (Kaution) are legally capped at three months' cold rent.

resources.title: Banking — Munich
resources.body: Opening a German current account (Girokonto) typically requires a registered address, so most newcomers complete the Anmeldung first. Both branch banks and app-based banks operate in Munich; a tax ID and residence permit help with full account features.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Munich
resources.body: Munich offers German public (state) schools plus a strong cluster of international schools serving expatriate families. International options teach English-medium and IB/British/American curricula alongside the Bavarian state system.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Munich
resources.body: New residents must register their address (Anmeldung) at the city's citizen office. Registration is mandatory, usually within two weeks of moving in, and produces the Meldebescheinigung needed for banking, tax and residence-permit steps.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Munich
resources.body: After registering, residents are issued a tax identification number automatically by post. Employees are assigned a tax class and file with the local tax office; the Steuer-ID is required for payroll and most financial services.

resources.title: Transport — Munich
resources.body: Munich has an extensive integrated public transport network (U-Bahn, S-Bahn, tram and bus) governed by a single fare union. The nationwide Deutschlandticket also covers local transit. Health coverage requires enrolling in statutory or private health insurance and choosing a GP (Hausarzt).

resources.title: Housing — Barcelona
resources.body: Barcelona has a competitive, high-demand rental market, especially in central districts (Eixample, Ciutat Vella, Gràcia). Furnished and unfurnished flats are common; a deposit plus first month's rent is typically required up front, and many landlords request proof of income or a guarantor. Most searches happen through online portals and local agencies.

resources.title: Banking — Barcelona
resources.body: Opening a resident bank account generally requires an NIE (foreigner ID number), passport, proof of address, and proof of employment or income. Non-resident accounts are also available with fewer documents. Major Spanish retail banks operate widely across the city with English-language support at larger branches.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Barcelona
resources.body: Barcelona offers public schools (instruction primarily in Catalan, with Spanish), concertados (state-subsidised private), and a broad range of international schools serving expatriate families. International options include British, American, French, German and International Baccalaureate curricula. Public school placement is tied to residential registration (empadronamiento).

resources.title: Registration & admin — Barcelona
resources.body: New residents must obtain an NIE and register on the municipal padrón (empadronamiento) at their local district office (Oficina d'Atenció Ciutadana) to prove local residence. The padrón certificate is required for many administrative steps including school enrolment and healthcare registration. EU/EEA citizens register on the Central Register of Foreigners; non-EU nationals require the appropriate residence authorisation.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Barcelona
resources.body: Individuals need a tax identification number to work and file taxes: Spanish nationals use the NIF, and foreigners use the NIE, which also serves as their tax identifier. Residents are taxed on worldwide income; Spain's national tax authority administers income tax (IRPF), with some devolved competencies at the Catalan regional level.

resources.title: Transport — Barcelona
resources.body: Barcelona has an extensive integrated public transport network covering metro, buses, trams and local trains, managed under a single fare-integration authority with zone-based ticketing. Rechargeable travel cards cover unlimited travel within a zone for a set period. EU/EEA driving licences are valid; many non-EU licences must be exchanged, and health coverage is accessed by registering for a regional public health card after empadronamiento.

resources.title: Housing — Madrid
resources.body: Madrid's rental market is competitive, especially in central districts (Centro, Salamanca, Chamberi). One-bedroom apartments in the centre are in high demand; expect to provide proof of income and often a guarantor. Idealista and Fotocasa are the dominant rental portals.

resources.title: Banking — Madrid
resources.body: Opening a Spanish bank account typically requires an NIE (foreigner ID number), passport, proof of address (empadronamiento) and proof of employment or income. Major retail banks include BBVA, Santander, CaixaBank and Sabadell; non-resident accounts are available at most branches before an NIE is issued.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Madrid
resources.body: Madrid offers a wide range of public (Spanish curriculum), bilingual, concertado (semi-private) and international schools. International options cover British, American, French, German and IB curricula, concentrated in the northern and western suburbs (e.g. Pozuelo, Las Rozas, Aravaca).

resources.title: Registration & admin — Madrid
resources.body: New residents must register on the municipal register (empadronamiento) at their local Junta Municipal or Padron office to obtain the certificado de empadronamiento, which is required for many administrative steps. EU citizens register with the Central Register of Foreigners; non-EU nationals need the appropriate residence permit and TIE card.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Madrid
resources.body: Individuals need a tax identification number to work and pay taxes: the NIE serves as the tax ID for foreigners, while Spanish nationals use the DNI/NIF. Income tax (IRPF) is administered nationally by the Agencia Tributaria (AEAT), with regional components applied by the Comunidad de Madrid.

resources.title: Transport — Madrid
resources.body: Madrid has an extensive integrated public transport network (metro, buses, Cercanias commuter rail and light rail) managed by the Consorcio Regional de Transportes de Madrid (CRTM). A rechargeable Tarjeta Transporte Publico is used for the Abono Transportes monthly pass. Under-26s pay a heavily discounted youth pass.

resources.title: Housing — Espoo
resources.body: Espoo is part of the Helsinki metropolitan area and has among the highest rents in Finland, slightly below Helsinki. One-bedroom flats in central districts such as Tapiola and Leppavaara typically rent for roughly EUR 900-1,100/month. Deposits of one to three months' rent are standard.

resources.title: Banking — Espoo
resources.body: Opening a Finnish bank account generally requires a Finnish personal identity code (henkilotunnus), a valid passport or national ID, a residence permit for non-EU/EEA nationals, and proof of address or employment. Major retail banks operating in Espoo include Nordea, OP (Osuuspankki), Danske Bank and S-Pankki.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Espoo
resources.body: Espoo provides Finnish- and Swedish-language comprehensive schools following the Finnish national core curriculum, plus English-language and international options such as Espoo International School and private IB schools. Schooling is compulsory and municipally organised.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Espoo
resources.body: New residents must register their move and obtain a Finnish personal identity code and municipality of residence at the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV). Non-EU/EEA nationals must first secure a residence permit from the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) before registering.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Espoo
resources.body: The Finnish Tax Administration (Vero) issues the tax card (verokortti) needed for employment and withholds progressive income tax. New arrivals request a tax card and, where relevant, a tax number from Vero once they have a personal identity code.

resources.title: Transport — Espoo
resources.body: Espoo is served by HSL (Helsinki Region Transport): buses, the Lansimetro metro extension, commuter trains and trams, all on one regional ticketing system shared with Helsinki and Vantaa. Zone fares apply (Espoo sits in zones B and C).

resources.title: Housing — Helsinki
resources.body: Helsinki has a competitive rental market. Most landlords require proof of income and ID. Average 1BR in city centre ~€1,100–1,400/month. Deposits typically 1–2 months' rent. Key portals: Vuokraovi.com, Oikotie Asunnot.

resources.title: Banking — Helsinki
resources.body: Major banks: Nordea, OP (Osuuspankki), Danske Bank, S-Pankki. Non-residents can open accounts with passport and Finnish personal identity code (henkilötunnus). Some banks require proof of address. Digital banks (Holvi, Revolut) available as alternatives.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Helsinki
resources.body: Helsinki has Finnish-medium and Swedish-medium public schools (free), plus international schools (fee-paying). Key international options: Helsinki International School, European School Helsinki, Deutsche Schule Helsinki. Curricula: Finnish national, IB, German.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Helsinki
resources.body: EU/EEA citizens must register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) to obtain a Finnish personal identity code (henkilötunnus). Non-EU nationals need a residence permit from Migri (Finnish Immigration Service) before registering. Registration at local Maistraatti/DVV office.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Helsinki
resources.body: Tax ID is the henkilötunnus (Finnish personal identity code). Employees receive a tax card (verokortti) from the Finnish Tax Administration (Vero). Register via OmaVero portal. Employer withholds income tax at source based on the tax card.

resources.title: Transport — Helsinki
resources.body: HSL (Helsingin seudun liikenne) operates metro, tram, bus, and commuter rail. Monthly regional pass (AB zones, city + Espoo): ~€59.40/month. Driving licence: EU licences valid; non-EU licences from most countries valid for 2 years after registering, then must exchange via Traficom.

resources.title: Housing — Jyvaskyla
resources.body: Jyvaskyla is a university city in Central Finland with a comparatively affordable rental market versus Helsinki. Most rentals are handled through national listing portals and private landlords; student housing (KOAS) is significant given the large student population. Furnished units are less common. Leases usually require a security deposit and proof of income.

resources.title: Banking — Jyvaskyla
resources.body: Opening a Finnish bank account typically requires a Finnish personal identity code, a valid passport/ID, proof of address, and often proof of employment or residence permit. Strong authentication (online banking credentials) is central to Finnish daily life for services and logins. Major banks operate branches in Jyvaskyla.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Jyvaskyla
resources.body: Public education follows the Finnish national core curriculum and is free, including comprehensive school (peruskoulu). English-language and international schooling options are limited compared with Helsinki, but some IB-track and English-medium provision exists at upper-secondary level. Early childhood education (varhaiskasvatus) is municipally organised.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Jyvaskyla
resources.body: New residents must register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) to obtain a Finnish personal identity code and register their municipality of residence. EU/EEA citizens register their right of residence; non-EU nationals need a residence permit from Migri before registration. Municipal services in Jyvaskyla are then accessed via the registered home municipality.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Jyvaskyla
resources.body: Workers must obtain a tax card (verokortti) from the Finnish Tax Administration (Vero) so the correct withholding rate is applied to salary. The tax card requires a personal identity code. Non-residents staying under six months may be taxed at source. Vero provides guidance and an online service (OmaVero) for tax matters.

resources.title: Transport — Jyvaskyla
resources.body: Local public transport in Jyvaskyla is operated as the Linkki bus network, covering the city and surrounding municipalities. Travel cards and mobile tickets are available with season/monthly options. The city is bike-friendly. EU/EEA driving licences are valid; non-EU licences may need to be exchanged within a set period. Healthcare is arranged through the wellbeing services county (Central Finland) with social insurance via Kela.

resources.title: Housing — Oulu
resources.body: Oulu has a comparatively affordable rental market versus Helsinki or Tampere, driven by a large student and tech-worker population (university and Nokia/technology hubs). Most rentals are unfurnished; leases are commonly open-ended or fixed-term. Deposits are typically one to two months' rent. Newcomers usually search via national rental portals or through student housing (PSOAS) if eligible.

resources.title: Banking — Oulu
resources.body: Opening a Finnish bank account generally requires a Finnish personal identity code (henkilotunnus), a valid passport or national ID, a residence permit or proof of right to reside, and often a proof of address or employment contract. Strong electronic identification (online banking credentials) is central to daily life in Finland and is issued by the bank once the account is opened.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Oulu
resources.body: Public education in Oulu follows the Finnish national core curriculum and is free, including comprehensive school (grades 1-9). English-medium and international schooling is available for expatriate families, including an international programme in the city. Municipal early childhood education (day care) is also provided. Placement is coordinated by the City of Oulu education services.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Oulu
resources.body: On arrival, foreign residents register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) to obtain a Finnish personal identity code (henkilotunnus) and to register their municipality of residence. EU/EEA citizens register their right of residence, while non-EU citizens first secure a residence permit from Migri (the Finnish Immigration Service). Registration underpins access to banking, healthcare, and tax services.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Oulu
resources.body: Income tax is administered by the Finnish Tax Administration (Vero). New workers must obtain a tax card (verokortti) specifying their withholding rate and provide it to their employer; without it, a higher default withholding applies. Non-residents may be taxed under separate rules. The personal identity code doubles as the individual's tax identifier.

resources.title: Transport — Oulu
resources.body: Oulu is known as a leading winter-cycling city with an extensive year-round cycling network, complemented by a municipal bus system covering the city and surrounding region. Single tickets and season/period passes are available via travel card and mobile app. Registered residents access public healthcare through the regional wellbeing services county after registering with a local health station.

resources.title: Housing — Tampere
resources.body: Tampere is Finland's third-largest city and a major student and tech hub, so rental demand is high, especially for centre (Keskusta) and Tammela apartments. Most rentals are unfurnished and secured via national listing portals; a written lease plus a security deposit is standard. Newcomers typically need a Finnish personal identity code and proof of income to be shortlisted by larger landlords such as VVO/Lumo and city-linked operators.

resources.title: Banking — Tampere
resources.body: Opening a Finnish bank account in Tampere generally requires a personal identity code (henkilotunnus), a valid passport/ID and often proof of address or employment. Banks issue online-banking credentials that double as strong e-identification (needed for many public services). Appointments are usually booked in advance at a branch.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Tampere
resources.body: Tampere provides comprehensive basic education (grades 1-9) organised by the city, plus early childhood education and upper-secondary options. International families can access English-medium and IB pathways in the region; the city education office administers school placement, which is normally tied to the family's registered address.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Tampere
resources.body: New residents register their move in Finland with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV), which issues or confirms the personal identity code and municipality of residence. Registration in the population information system is the gateway to most other services (banking, tax, healthcare). EU/EEA citizens and non-EU nationals follow different pre-registration steps (EU registration vs. residence permit).

resources.title: Tax & finance — Tampere
resources.body: Employees and residents obtain a tax card (verokortti) from the Finnish Tax Administration (Vero) before starting work, so the correct withholding rate is applied. The personal identity code serves as the tax identifier for individuals; tax matters are managed via the MyTax (OmaVero) online service.

resources.title: Transport — Tampere
resources.body: Tampere's public transport is run under the Nysse brand, covering the city tram line and regional buses across the Tampere region. Fares use a zone-based season/value ticket loaded onto a travel card or the Nysse mobile app. Newcomers exchanging a foreign driving licence and registering for healthcare do so through the relevant national/regional authorities once they hold a personal identity code.

resources.title: Housing — Turku
resources.body: Turku's rental market is smaller and cheaper than Helsinki. Most rentals are found through online portals and require a Finnish personal identity code (henkilotunnus) and often proof of income or employment. Furnished units are less common; deposits are typically 1-2 months' rent. Student housing (TYS) is widely available given the large university population.

resources.title: Banking — Turku
resources.body: Opening a Finnish bank account generally requires a passport/ID, a residence permit or proof of legal residence, a Finnish personal identity code (henkilotunnus), and often proof of address or employment. Strong customer authentication and online banking credentials (verkkopankkitunnukset) are central to daily life in Finland. Major banks operate branches in Turku.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Turku
resources.body: Turku offers public Finnish- and Swedish-language schooling (Turku is officially bilingual) plus international options. Turku International School provides English-language instruction, and IB programmes are available in the region. Public basic education is free.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Turku
resources.body: New residents register their move and obtain a Finnish personal identity code (henkilotunnus) through the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV). EU/EEA citizens register their right of residence; non-EU nationals need a residence permit from Migri before registering. Local registration establishes access to municipal services.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Turku
resources.body: Employees must obtain a tax card (verokortti) from the Finnish Tax Administration (Vero) so the correct withholding rate is applied to salary. Newly arrived foreign workers may need to visit a tax office in person. Taxation is administered nationally, so the process in Turku is the same as elsewhere in Finland.

resources.title: Transport — Turku
resources.body: Turku's regional public transport is operated under the Foli brand, covering buses across Turku and neighbouring municipalities, plus the Fori city ferry across the Aura river. Tickets use a rechargeable travel card or mobile app. Monthly season tickets are available at resident rates. Non-EU/EEA driving licences generally must be exchanged within a limited period after establishing residence.

resources.title: Housing — Vantaa
resources.body: Vantaa is part of the Greater Helsinki metropolitan area and home to Helsinki Airport, so rents sit below central Helsinki but above the national average. Furnished and unfurnished one-bedroom flats are common near rail hubs like Tikkurila and Myyrmaki. Long-term leases usually run 12 months and most listings are in Finnish; a Finnish personal identity code and proof of income are typically expected before a landlord will sign.

resources.title: Banking — Vantaa
resources.body: Opening a Finnish bank account requires a residence permit (for non-EU citizens), a Finnish personal identity code, and identity documents. Banks apply strong identity verification and may take extra time for newcomers before granting online banking credentials, which double as a widely used e-identification tool. Major retail banks operate branches across the Helsinki region including Vantaa.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Vantaa
resources.body: Public comprehensive education follows the Finnish national curriculum and is free. Vantaa offers Finnish- and Swedish-language schools plus English-medium and international options within commuting distance in the Helsinki region, including IB programmes. Early childhood education (varhaiskasvatus) is subsidised and income-based.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Vantaa
resources.body: New residents register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) to obtain a Finnish personal identity code and register their municipality of residence. EU/EEA citizens staying over three months register their right of residence with Finnish Immigration Service; non-EU nationals need a residence permit first. The personal identity code unlocks banking, healthcare and tax services.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Vantaa
resources.body: Anyone working in Finland must obtain a tax card (verokortti) from the Finnish Tax Administration (Vero), which sets the withholding rate applied by employers. Newcomers request a tax card in person or online once they hold a personal identity code. Finland taxes worldwide income for tax residents; short-term workers may fall under a flat tax-at-source scheme.

resources.title: Transport — Vantaa
resources.body: Vantaa is served by HSL (Helsinki Region Transport), covering buses, trams, metro, commuter trains and the Ring Rail Line connecting the city and Helsinki Airport. A single regional ticket works across all modes, and monthly season tickets are zone-based. Public transport is extensive, reducing the need for a car.

resources.title: Housing — Lyon
resources.body: Lyon's rental market is competitive, especially in central arrondissements (1er, 2e, 6e Presqu'ile and Part-Dieu). One-bedroom apartments in the centre typically rent in the low four-figure euro range. Landlords usually require a French guarantor or a Visale guarantee, proof of income (payslips ~3x rent), and often use an agency (frais d'agence). Furnished (meuble) and unfurnished lets have different lease terms.

resources.title: Banking — Lyon
resources.body: Opening a French bank account requires proof of identity, proof of address (justificatif de domicile), and often a residence permit or long-stay visa. Major retail banks and online banks operate in Lyon. Newcomers frequently use online banks for faster onboarding while awaiting a proof of address.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Lyon
resources.body: Lyon has a strong public school system plus several international and bilingual options serving relocating families. International curricula are available through dedicated international schools; the Cite Scolaire Internationale de Lyon offers international sections within the public system. Enrolment in public schools is tied to the family's address (sectorisation).

resources.title: Registration & admin — Lyon
resources.body: Non-EU arrivals must validate their long-stay visa (VLS-TS) with the OFII and, where required, hold a residence permit (titre de sejour) handled via the local prefecture (Prefecture du Rhone). EU nationals do not need a residence permit but should register locally for services. Many administrative steps are handled online.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Lyon
resources.body: Residents are liable for French income tax and must obtain a tax identification number (numero fiscal / SPI) to file a return and access the online tax portal. Income tax is collected at source (prelevement a la source). New residents typically register with the tax administration after arrival.

resources.title: Transport — Lyon
resources.body: Lyon has an extensive public transport network operated by TCL, covering metro, tram, funicular, and buses, complemented by the Velo'v bike-share scheme. Monthly passes are available at reduced rates for young people and students. Non-EU driving licences may need to be exchanged for a French licence depending on the country of issue and reciprocity agreements; healthcare access requires registering with the French social security system to obtain a carte Vitale.

resources.title: Housing — London
resources.body: London has an expensive, fast-moving rental market. One-bedroom flats in central zones command premium rents; letting agents typically require references, proof of income (often 2.5-3x monthly rent), a right-to-rent immigration check, and a holding deposit. Most tenancies are Assured Shorthold Tenancies (ASTs).

resources.title: Banking — London
resources.body: Opening a UK current account usually requires proof of identity and proof of a UK address; newcomers without an address history often use digital banks or basic accounts first. Standard high-street banks offer current accounts once documentation is provided.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — London
resources.body: London offers state (free, catchment/admissions-based), academy, faith, and a large private/independent sector, plus numerous international schools serving expatriate families. State school places are allocated through the local borough council admissions process.

resources.title: Registration & admin — London
resources.body: The UK has no universal residents' registration office; local administration is handled by borough councils (e.g. council tax registration). Immigration status is managed centrally through UK Visas and Immigration, and newcomers register with local services (council, GP) after arrival.

resources.title: Tax & finance — London
resources.body: Income tax and National Insurance are administered by HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). Employees are typically taxed at source via PAYE; new arrivals need a National Insurance number to work and may need to register with HMRC.

resources.title: Transport — London
resources.body: London's integrated public transport network is run by Transport for London (TfL), covering the Underground, Overground, Elizabeth line, buses, DLR, trams and river services. Fares use a zonal system with contactless/Oyster pay-as-you-go capping; monthly Travelcards are available by zone range.

resources.title: Housing — Manchester
resources.body: Manchester's rental market is competitive, especially in the city centre and areas like Ancoats, Northern Quarter, and Salford Quays. Tenancies are typically Assured Shorthold Tenancies (AST), commonly 12 months. Landlords/agents usually require referencing, proof of income, and a security deposit protected in a government-approved scheme.

resources.title: Banking — Manchester
resources.body: Opening a UK current account generally requires proof of identity and proof of UK address. Newcomers can use high-street banks or app-based banks (which often accept fewer documents). Some banks offer accounts geared toward new arrivals without a long address history.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Manchester
resources.body: State schooling in Manchester is free and allocated by catchment/admissions criteria via the local authority. Independent and international options exist for families wanting alternative curricula. Applications for state school places go through Manchester City Council admissions.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Manchester
resources.body: The UK has no continental-style residential registration. Newcomers typically confirm status via a Biometric Residence Permit (BRP) or eVisa, register with a local GP, and apply for a National Insurance Number for work. Address is evidenced through tenancy and utility documents rather than a civil registry.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Manchester
resources.body: Income tax and National Insurance are administered by HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC), generally deducted at source through PAYE for employees. New workers should obtain a National Insurance Number and may need to verify their tax code with HMRC.

resources.title: Transport — Manchester
resources.body: Manchester is served by an integrated network of Metrolink trams, buses (now under the Bee Network franchising), and local/regional rail. Contactless and capped fares are widely available. Season tickets and travelcards cover tram/bus zones across Greater Manchester.

resources.title: Housing — Cork
resources.body: Cork's rental market is tight, especially in the city centre and near University College Cork; supply is limited and viewings are competitive. Most listings run through online portals, and tenancies are registered with the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB). Expect to provide references, proof of employment, and a deposit up front.

resources.title: Banking — Cork
resources.body: Opening a current account typically requires photo ID (passport or national ID), proof of Irish address, and often a PPS number. Some banks allow non-resident or newcomer account opening with limited documentation initially. Following market exits by Ulster Bank and KBC, the main retail banks are AIB, Bank of Ireland, and Permanent TSB; digital options like Revolut and N26 are widely used.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Cork
resources.body: Cork offers public (state-funded) primary and post-primary schools following the Irish national curriculum, culminating in the Junior Cycle and Leaving Certificate. Places are allocated by enrolment policy, often with waiting lists. International and private options exist but are limited compared with Dublin.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Cork
resources.body: EU/EEA/Swiss nationals have the right to live and work in Ireland without registration. Non-EEA nationals must register their immigration permission and obtain an Irish Residence Permit (IRP); outside Dublin this is handled at the local Garda National Immigration Bureau registration office.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Cork
resources.body: Workers need a Personal Public Service (PPS) number to be employed and taxed correctly; without it, emergency tax rates apply. Income tax is administered via the PAYE system, and employees should register their employment and claim tax credits through Revenue's myAccount.

resources.title: Transport — Cork
resources.body: Cork is served by Bus Éireann city routes under the Transport for Ireland (TFI) brand, plus commuter rail via Kent Station. The TFI Leap Card provides discounted pay-as-you-go fares and fare capping. The city is compact and walkable, with cycling infrastructure expanding.

resources.title: Housing — Dublin
resources.body: Dublin's rental market is tight and expensive, with strong demand and low supply. One-bedroom apartments in the city centre command premium rents. Tenancies are typically secured through online portals, and a security deposit plus first month's rent is standard at move-in.

resources.title: Banking — Dublin
resources.body: Opening a current account in Dublin generally requires photo ID and proof of an Irish address; a PPS number is often requested. Digital banks are widely used by newcomers as they can be opened quickly before local address documents are available.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Dublin
resources.body: Dublin offers state-funded primary and secondary schools following the Irish national curriculum, alongside a number of private and international schools. Non-Irish curricula are available at international schools serving the expatriate community.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Dublin
resources.body: EU/EEA/Swiss citizens may live and work in Ireland without registration. Non-EEA nationals staying more than 90 days must register their immigration permission and obtain an Irish Residence Permit (IRP).

resources.title: Tax & finance — Dublin
resources.body: Anyone starting work or accessing public services in Ireland needs a Personal Public Service (PPS) number. Income tax and social contributions are administered through the national revenue authority under the PAYE system.

resources.title: Transport — Dublin
resources.body: Dublin's public transport is coordinated under Transport for Ireland and includes Dublin Bus, the Luas tram network, and the DART/commuter rail. Fares are paid with the contactless Leap Card, which offers capped and discounted travel.

resources.title: Housing — Bengaluru
resources.body: Bengaluru's rental market is competitive, especially in tech-hub areas like Koramangala, Indiranagar, Whitefield and HSR Layout. One-bedroom flats in central/prime areas command a premium and security deposits are notoriously high compared with the rest of India, often equal to several months of rent. Rental agreements are typically 11-month leases and most tenancies go through brokers or online platforms.

resources.title: Banking — Bengaluru
resources.body: Opening a resident or NRO/NRE bank account requires standard KYC. Foreign nationals typically need a passport, valid visa, proof of local address and a PAN card. Major private and public banks operate extensive branch and ATM networks across the city.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Bengaluru
resources.body: Bengaluru has a large selection of international and private schools serving expatriate and local families, concentrated around Whitefield, Sarjapur Road and North Bengaluru near the airport. Options span multiple curricula and admissions are competitive with waitlists at popular schools.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Bengaluru
resources.body: Foreign nationals staying in India beyond 180 days on certain visa categories must register with the local Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) within 14 days of arrival. Bengaluru has an FRRO office and registration is handled online with an in-person appointment.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Bengaluru
resources.body: Anyone earning income or opening financial accounts in India needs a PAN (Permanent Account Number) issued by the Income Tax Department. Tax residency is determined by days of physical presence in India, and residents are taxed on worldwide income while non-residents are taxed on Indian-source income.

resources.title: Transport — Bengaluru
resources.body: Bengaluru is served by BMTC city buses and the expanding Namma Metro rail network, supplemented by app-based cabs and auto-rickshaws. Traffic congestion is significant, so many residents rely on the metro for cross-city commuting. Foreign residents can convert a valid foreign driving licence to an Indian licence through the regional transport office.

resources.title: Housing — Delhi
resources.body: Delhi's rental market spans a wide range: central and expat-favoured areas like South Delhi (Vasant Vihar, Greater Kailash, Defence Colony) and central New Delhi command high rents, while suburbs (Dwarka, Rohini) and NCR cities (Gurgaon/Gurugram, Noida) are more affordable. Furnished flats are common for expats. Deposits are typically 2-3 months' rent (higher for premium/independent houses). Brokers usually charge one month's rent as commission. Lease agreements are commonly 11 months to avoid rent-control registration.

resources.title: Banking — Delhi
resources.body: Foreign nationals resident in India can open a resident savings account; non-residents use NRE/NRO accounts. Banks apply full KYC. Popular banks with expat services include HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, State Bank of India (SBI), Axis Bank, and international banks like Citibank, HSBC and Standard Chartered. A PAN card and valid visa/residence permit are generally required.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Delhi
resources.body: Delhi and the surrounding NCR host many international schools serving expat families, offering IB, British (IGCSE/A-level) and American curricula alongside the Indian CBSE and ICSE boards. Well-known options include The British School New Delhi, The American Embassy School, Pathways schools, and various IB World Schools. Admission is competitive and often requires advance application.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Delhi
resources.body: Foreign nationals staying in India beyond 180 days on long-term visas (employment, student, research, etc.) must register with the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) in Delhi, generally within 14 days of arrival. Registration is done online via the e-FRRO portal and produces a Residential Permit. Address changes and visa extensions are also processed through FRRO/e-FRRO.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Delhi
resources.body: India levies income tax administered by the Income Tax Department under the Central Board of Direct Taxes. Residency for tax purposes is determined by days of physical presence (the 182-day rule and related tests). Every taxpayer needs a Permanent Account Number (PAN); salaried employees have tax withheld at source (TDS). Foreign nationals should also assess tax-residency and any double-taxation treaty relief.

resources.title: Transport — Delhi
resources.body: Delhi has an extensive public transport network anchored by the Delhi Metro (operated by DMRC), supplemented by DTC buses, autorickshaws, and app-based cabs (Uber/Ola). The Metro uses smart cards and QR tickets; a common mobility card is available. Traffic congestion is significant, so many expats rely on the Metro plus ride-hailing. Foreign licence holders can drive on an International Driving Permit short-term but should convert to an Indian licence for longer stays.

resources.title: Housing — Mumbai
resources.body: Mumbai is India's most expensive rental market. Expats typically rent furnished flats in areas like Bandra, Powai, Lower Parel, and Worli. Leases usually run 11 months (to avoid stamp-duty rules on 12-month registration) and often require brokerage of one month's rent plus stamp duty and registration on the leave-and-license agreement. Landlords frequently prefer company leases for corporate tenants.

resources.title: Banking — Mumbai
resources.body: Foreign nationals resident in India can open resident savings accounts; non-residents use NRE/NRO accounts. Major banks include HDFC, ICICI, SBI, Axis, and Kotak Mahindra, plus international banks like HSBC, Citi, and Standard Chartered. Account opening requires KYC documentation and is generally straightforward once a PAN and local address proof are available.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Mumbai
resources.body: Mumbai has a wide range of international and private schools serving expat families, concentrated in South Mumbai, Bandra, Powai, and the western suburbs. Admissions are competitive and often require early application; fees at international schools are among the highest in India.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Mumbai
resources.body: Foreign nationals on long-stay visas (employment, student, etc.) valid for more than 180 days must register with the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) in Mumbai, typically within 14 days of arrival, via the e-FRRO online portal. Registration produces a residential permit and is required for many downstream services.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Mumbai
resources.body: India taxes residents on worldwide income; tax residency is determined by days of physical presence (generally 182 days or more in a financial year, with additional tests). A Permanent Account Number (PAN) is mandatory for salary, banking, and property transactions. The financial year runs April to March, and returns are typically due by 31 July for individuals.

resources.title: Transport — Mumbai
resources.body: Mumbai's public transport is dominated by the suburban railway network ('local trains'), supplemented by BEST buses, an expanding Metro network, monorail, black-and-yellow taxis, autorickshaws (in the suburbs), and app-based cabs. Suburban trains are the backbone of daily commuting.

resources.title: Housing — Florence
resources.body: No municipal rental portal; the private long-term market runs through national listing portals and local agencies. Leases (contratto di locazione) are commonly 4+4 years; deposit typically 1-3 months. Rents quoted in EUR. Register the lease with the Agenzia delle Entrate and provide a codice fiscale to sign.

resources.title: Banking — Florence
resources.body: No city-level banking authority. Newcomers open accounts with national banks operating branches in Florence. A codice fiscale plus valid ID and proof of address are typically required for a resident account. Amounts in EUR.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Florence
resources.body: State-school enrolment is handled under the Italian national system (Ministero dell'Istruzione); the Comune di Firenze runs municipal nurseries (nidi 0-3), infant schools and school services. International/bilingual options exist but are more limited than Milan/Rome.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Florence
resources.body: Residence registration (residenza anagrafica) and civil-status admin are handled by the Comune di Firenze (Anagrafe). Non-EU nationals also process a permesso di soggiorno via the Questura; EU citizens staying over 3 months complete iscrizione anagrafica.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Florence
resources.body: Personal taxation is administered nationally by the Agenzia delle Entrate; the codice fiscale is the universal tax identifier. National IRPEF applies with regional (Toscana) and municipal (Comune di Firenze) surcharges. Local property/waste taxes (IMU, TARI) are handled by the Comune. Currency EUR.

resources.title: Transport — Florence
resources.body: Urban and suburban bus service in the Florence area is operated under the regional Autolinee Toscane concession; Florence also has tram lines and regional/national rail via Trenitalia. Fares in EUR. Airport: Florence Amerigo Vespucci (FLR).

resources.title: Housing — Genoa
resources.body: Rental market centred on portals and local agencies; typical urban rents in EUR. Long-term leases (contratto di locazione) commonly 4+4 years; deposit usually 1-3 months.

resources.title: Banking — Genoa
resources.body: Retail banks with branches in Genoa. Codice fiscale and proof of address/residence typically required to open a resident account.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Genoa
resources.body: State schools managed under the Italian national system; international/bilingual options are limited relative to Milan/Rome.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Genoa
resources.body: Residence registration and municipal admin handled by the Comune di Genova; immigration formalities via Questura/Prefettura.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Genoa
resources.body: Personal taxation administered nationally by the Agenzia delle Entrate; codice fiscale is the universal tax identifier.

resources.title: Transport — Genoa
resources.body: Urban public transport operated by AMT Genova: buses, metro, funiculars, lifts and the Genova-Casella narrow-gauge railway; regional/national rail via Trenitalia.

resources.title: Housing — Milan
resources.body: Milan is Italy's most expensive rental market; central one-bedroom flats are in high demand and typically require a deposit plus first month upfront. Contracts are usually the 4+4 canone libero or 3+2 canone concordato type.

resources.title: Banking — Milan
resources.body: Opening a resident bank account requires an Italian tax code (codice fiscale) and proof of address; non-residents can open a conto non residente with a passport. Digital banks are widely used by newcomers before residency is finalised.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Milan
resources.body: Milan has a broad range of international schools serving expatriate families, offering English-language and multilingual curricula alongside Italian state and private schools. Places at popular international schools should be secured well in advance.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Milan
resources.body: EU nationals staying over three months register residence with the local Comune (anagrafe); non-EU nationals must obtain a permesso di soggiorno after entry. Residence registration triggers issuance of a residence certificate and access to local services.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Milan
resources.body: Everyone needs a codice fiscale (Italian tax identification number) for employment, banking, renting and healthcare. It is issued by the Agenzia delle Entrate and required for almost all administrative processes.

resources.title: Transport — Milan
resources.body: Milan has an extensive integrated public transport network of metro, trams and buses operated by ATM, plus regional and suburban rail. Newcomers can exchange certain foreign driving licences and must register with the regional health service for medical care.

resources.title: Housing — Pisa
resources.body: Pisa is a mid-sized Tuscan university city; asking rents in the historic centre (Centro Storico) average roughly EUR 13 per square metre per month, so a small one-bedroom flat typically runs about EUR 500-700/month. The main online rental portals are Idealista (https://www.idealista.it/affitto-case/pisa/) and Immobiliare.it. Under Italian tenancy law (Law 392/1978) the security deposit is commonly capped at a maximum of three months' rent.

resources.title: Banking — Pisa
resources.body: Newcomers open an account with a major retail bank; the largest networks present in Pisa are Intesa Sanpaolo, UniCredit and Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena (headquartered in nearby Siena, Tuscany). To open an account a foreigner needs a valid passport or national ID, an Italian codice fiscale (tax code) and proof of address; a resident account additionally requires a residence permit or work contract (source: https://yourwaytoitaly.it/en/articles/how-to-open-a-bank-account-in-italy-as-a-foreigner).

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Pisa
resources.body: Pisa has no verified dedicated English-curriculum international school within the comune; families relocating with school-age children typically look to international options in the wider Tuscany region (e.g. Florence). No corridor-verified Pisa international school listing was available at time of harvest.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Pisa
resources.body: On moving to Pisa a newcomer must register their residence (variazione di residenza / iscrizione anagrafica) with the Ufficio Anagrafe of the Comune di Pisa, within 20 days of the move. EU citizens register residence directly; non-EU nationals must first hold a valid permesso di soggiorno before registering. Authority: Comune di Pisa - Anagrafe.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Pisa
resources.body: For individuals the Italian tax identifier is the Codice Fiscale, issued by the Agenzia delle Entrate. In Pisa it is handled by the Direzione Provinciale di Pisa (Galleria Giovan Battista Gerace 7, 56124 Pisa). The codice fiscale is required to open a bank account, sign a lease, register with the health service and be employed.

resources.title: Transport — Pisa
resources.body: Regional and city bus services in Pisa are operated by Autolinee Toscane (brand 'at'; https://www.at-bus.it). A dedicated automated 'PisaMover' people-mover connects Pisa Centrale station to Pisa International Airport. A corridor-verified price for the Pisa urban monthly pass was not available at harvest. EU/EEA driving licences remain valid; non-EU residents must generally convert to an Italian licence within one year of establishing residence.

resources.title: Housing — Rome
resources.body: Rome's rental market is competitive, especially in central rioni (Centro Storico, Trastevere, Prati). Long-term leases (contratto di locazione) typically run 4+4 years; furnished short/medium-term options are common for relocating employees. A landlord usually requires proof of income, ID/codice fiscale, and often a guarantor. Idealista, Immobiliare.it and agency listings dominate the market.

resources.title: Banking — Rome
resources.body: Opening a resident bank account (conto corrente) requires a codice fiscale, valid ID/passport, and proof of address; residence registration helps. Major retail banks include Intesa Sanpaolo, UniCredit, BPER and BNL, alongside digital options. Non-residents can open a conto non residente with more limited features until residency is established.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Rome
resources.body: Rome has a broad range of international and bilingual schools serving relocating families, offering British, American and IB curricula, plus French, German and other national systems. Places at popular international schools can be limited, so early application is advised. Italian state schools follow the national curriculum in Italian.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Rome
resources.body: EU/EEA nationals staying beyond 3 months register their residence (residenza) with the Comune di Roma anagrafe; non-EU nationals must first obtain a permesso di soggiorno via the Questura/post office kit and then register residence. The codice fiscale is needed for almost all administrative steps.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Rome
resources.body: The codice fiscale is the Italian tax identification code, required for employment, banking, renting and most contracts; it is issued by the Agenzia delle Entrate. Tax residents are generally taxed on worldwide income; special regimes (e.g. impatriati / inbound worker relief) may apply to qualifying relocating employees.

resources.title: Transport — Rome
resources.body: Rome's public transport is run by ATAC and includes three metro lines (A, B/B1, C), extensive buses, trams and urban rail, integrated under the Metrebus ticketing system. A monthly pass covers metro, bus and tram within the city. Non-EU licence holders must generally exchange or re-sit for an Italian licence, while EU/EEA licences are broadly valid; healthcare access is via registration with the local ASL for the Servizio Sanitario Nazionale.

resources.title: Housing — Turin
resources.body: Turin is a comparatively affordable major-Italian-city rental market; a 1-bedroom apartment in the city centre is cited at roughly EUR 700-950/month (Numbeo lists a central 1-bed at about EUR 771/month; HousingAnywhere cites an overall average near EUR 940). The main online rental portals are Immobiliare.it and Idealista.it. Italian law does not impose a single national deposit cap as in Switzerland; the security deposit (cauzione) is customary and typically ranges from 1 to 3 months' rent, commonly up to 3.

resources.title: Banking — Turin
resources.body: A newcomer opens a conto corrente (bank account) in person at a local branch. Typical documents required: a valid passport/national ID, an Italian codice fiscale (tax code), proof of address/residence in Italy, and for non-EU nationals a valid permesso di soggiorno (residence permit). Major banks with a strong Turin presence include Intesa Sanpaolo (headquartered in Turin) and UniCredit. Note: a single authoritative source page for the exact document checklist was not verified, so this block is flagged source_missing.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Turin
resources.body: International schooling in Turin is anchored by the International School of Turin (IST), an authorised IB World School since 1963 offering the full IB Continuum (PYP, MYP, IB Diploma) in English (https://www.isturin.it/). A directory of international schools in and around Turin is maintained at https://www.international-schools-database.com/in/turin.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Turin
resources.body: On moving to Turin a newcomer must file a 'dichiarazione di residenza' (declaration of residence) with the Comune di Torino civil-registry office (Anagrafe) within 20 days of taking up residence; non-EU nationals must also hold a valid permesso di soggiorno (residence permit). The municipality then completes the anagrafic registration.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Turin
resources.body: Individuals need a codice fiscale (Italian tax identification code), issued by the Agenzia delle Entrate. EU and non-EU foreign citizens applying for their first codice fiscale must book an in-person appointment at an Agenzia delle Entrate office; in Turin this is handled by the Direzione Provinciale di Torino. The code identifies the taxpayer to the Italian tax authority.

resources.title: Transport — Turin
resources.body: Public transport in Turin is operated by Gruppo Torinese Trasporti (GTT). The current official monthly urban ('Formula U') pass price could not be verified from an official GTT source (the GTT tariff pages returned an error), so monthly_pass_price is left null rather than invented. Driving: EU/EEA licences remain valid in Italy; a non-EU licence holder may drive for up to one year from acquiring residenza anagrafica, after which the licence must be exchanged (only where a reciprocity agreement with Italy exists) or an Italian licence obtained by examination (https://www.esteri.it/en/servizi-opportunita/italiani-all-estero/autoveicoli_e_patenti/patenteguida/). Healthcare: new residents access public healthcare by registering with the Servizio Sanitario Nazionale (SSN) at the local ASL and choosing a medico di base (family doctor); those resident under three months generally cannot enrol.

resources.title: Housing — Amsterdam
resources.body: Amsterdam has an extremely tight and expensive rental market, with high demand and limited supply. Newcomers typically use lettings agencies (makelaars) or online portals; furnished and short-stay options carry a premium. Registration at a rental address is required to obtain a BSN, so a genuine rental contract permitting registration is essential.

resources.title: Banking — Amsterdam
resources.body: Opening a Dutch bank account generally requires a BSN, proof of address, passport/ID and often proof of employment. Major banks offer expat-friendly onboarding; digital banks are common alternatives for arrivals awaiting a BSN. An iDEAL-capable Dutch account is important for everyday payments.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Amsterdam
resources.body: Amsterdam offers Dutch public schools, bilingual (TTO) streams, and several international schools serving expat families. Dutch-subsidised international education and private international schools follow varied curricula; places are limited and waiting lists common, so early application is advised.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Amsterdam
resources.body: New residents must register with the municipality (Gemeente Amsterdam) at their address, which triggers issuance of a BSN. EU/EEA nationals register directly; non-EU nationals typically arrange residence/work authorisation via the IND before or alongside registration. Bring passport, birth certificate (often legalised/translated) and proof of address.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Amsterdam
resources.body: Income tax and social contributions are administered by the Belastingdienst. Employees are taxed via payroll withholding; the BSN is used for all tax matters. Qualifying skilled migrants may be eligible for the 30% ruling, a significant expat tax advantage that must be applied for.

resources.title: Transport — Amsterdam
resources.body: Amsterdam has an extensive public transport network of trams, buses, metro and ferries operated primarily by GVB, plus national rail (NS). Payment uses the OV-chipkaart or contactless bank card/OVpay. Cycling is a dominant mode of transport across the city.

resources.title: Housing — Rotterdam
resources.body: Rotterdam's rental market is competitive but generally more affordable than Amsterdam. Most listings are found via online portals and agents (makelaars); furnished and unfurnished options both common. Expats often use rental agencies, and many landlords require proof of income (typically 3-4x monthly rent) and Dutch bank account details.

resources.title: Banking — Rotterdam
resources.body: Opening a Dutch bank account typically requires a BSN (citizen service number), proof of address (registration), passport/ID, and sometimes proof of employment. Major banks offer expat-friendly onboarding; some digital banks allow account opening before BSN issuance.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Rotterdam
resources.body: Rotterdam offers Dutch public schools, bilingual programs, and several international schools serving the expat community. International options follow British, IB, and other curricula. Public education is free or low-cost; international schools charge tuition.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Rotterdam
resources.body: New residents staying longer than four months must register with the municipality (Gemeente Rotterdam) to receive a BSN. EU/EEA citizens register directly; non-EU nationals typically need a residence permit (IND) first. Registration requires a rental contract or proof of address and a valid ID.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Rotterdam
resources.body: Income tax is administered nationally by the Belastingdienst (Dutch Tax Administration). Residents are taxed on worldwide income; qualifying skilled migrants may benefit from the 30% ruling. The BSN doubles as the tax identification number.

resources.title: Transport — Rotterdam
resources.body: Rotterdam has an extensive public transport network run by RET, covering metro, tram, and bus lines, integrated with regional rail. Travel uses the OV-chipkaart (or contactless/OVpay). The city is highly bike-friendly with dedicated cycling infrastructure.

resources.title: Housing — Bergen
resources.body: Bergen has a tight rental market driven by students and energy-sector workers; most listings are found on Finn.no. Rentals are typically unfurnished or semi-furnished, and landlords generally require a deposit held in a separate tenancy deposit account (depositumskonto).

resources.title: Banking — Bergen
resources.body: To open a Norwegian bank account you generally need a D-number or national identity number (fodselsnummer), valid ID/passport, and proof of address or an employment contract. Common banks in Bergen include DNB, Nordea, and the regional Sparebanken Vest, which is headquartered in Bergen.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Bergen
resources.body: Bergen offers Norwegian public schooling (free, tuition-funded by residence) as well as international options; the International School of Bergen provides an English-language IB-oriented curriculum for expat families.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Bergen
resources.body: New arrivals must legalise their stay (EU/EEA nationals register with the police; non-EEA nationals apply for a residence permit via UDI), then register with the National Population Register (Folkeregisteret) administered by the Norwegian Tax Administration to obtain a national identity number.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Bergen
resources.body: Residents need a tax deduction card (skattekort) from the Norwegian Tax Administration (Skatteetaten). A D-number is issued for temporary stays and a national identity number (fodselsnummer) for those registered as residents.

resources.title: Transport — Bergen
resources.body: Public transport in Bergen is run by Skyss and includes the Bybanen light rail, buses, and city ferries. Tickets and monthly passes are managed via the Skyss app or travel card. EU/EEA driving licences can generally be used or exchanged without a test; healthcare access requires registering with a regular GP (fastlege).

resources.title: Housing — Oslo
resources.body: Oslo's rental market is competitive and among the most expensive in Norway; most listings are found via online portals and demand moves quickly, especially for central one-bedroom flats. Deposits are held in a dedicated tenant deposit account (depositumskonto).

resources.title: Banking — Oslo
resources.body: Opening a Norwegian bank account requires a national identity number or D-number plus valid ID; account opening for newcomers typically follows registration with the tax authority. BankID is the standard digital identity used for banking and public services.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Oslo
resources.body: Oslo offers Norwegian public schooling (free) as well as international schools serving expatriate families with English-language and international curricula. Public school placement is generally tied to the residential catchment area.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Oslo
resources.body: EU/EEA nationals register with the police, while non-EEA nationals need a residence permit before arrival. Newcomers must report to the tax office for an ID check and register in the National Population Register to obtain a national identity number or D-number.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Oslo
resources.body: Everyone working in Norway needs a tax deduction card (skattekort) and a national identity number or D-number. Income tax is administered by the Norwegian Tax Administration (Skatteetaten), which issues the tax card based on expected income.

resources.title: Transport — Oslo
resources.body: Oslo has an integrated public transport network covering metro (T-bane), trams, buses and local ferries, operated under a single ticketing system with zone-based fares. Tickets and passes are bought via a mobile app or travel card.

resources.title: Housing — Singapore
resources.body: Singapore's rental market is expensive and fast-moving. Expats typically rent private condominiums or HDB flats; a central-district (Core Central Region: Orchard, River Valley, Tanjong Pagar) one-bedroom condo commands premium rents. Standard leases run 12-24 months. The market is dominated by agents and portals like PropertyGuru and 99.co.

resources.title: Banking — Singapore
resources.body: Opening a bank account is straightforward for residents holding an Employment Pass or S Pass. Major banks are DBS/POSB, OCBC, and UOB, alongside international banks like Standard Chartered, HSBC, and Citibank. Foreigners generally need passport, work pass, proof of address, and sometimes a minimum initial deposit.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Singapore
resources.body: Singapore has a large international school sector serving expat families, offering IB, British, American, and other national curricula. Well-known international schools include UWCSEA, Tanglin Trust School, Singapore American School, and Dulwich College. Local public schools follow the Singapore national curriculum but have limited places for foreigners. Demand is high and waiting lists are common.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Singapore
resources.body: Foreign workers must hold a valid work pass (Employment Pass, S Pass, or Work Permit) issued by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) before working. After arrival, pass holders complete registration and receive their pass card; those staying long-term may register for identification. The employer typically sponsors and initiates the pass application.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Singapore
resources.body: Income tax is administered by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS). Singapore has a progressive resident income tax system with relatively low rates and no capital gains tax. Tax residency generally depends on days present in the country. Individuals are identified for tax by their NRIC (locals/PRs) or FIN (foreigners on passes).

resources.title: Transport — Singapore
resources.body: Singapore has an extensive, efficient public transport network of MRT (metro) and buses, operated under a unified fare system. Travelers pay via contactless bank cards or the EZ-Link/SimplyGo stored-value card. Car ownership is very expensive due to the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system. Foreigners can drive on a valid foreign or international licence short-term, then must convert to a Singapore licence.

resources.title: Housing — Los Angeles
resources.body: Los Angeles has an expensive, competitive rental market. Leases are typically 12 months; landlords require proof of income (often 2.5-3x rent), credit check, and references. Rents are highest on the Westside and downtown; more affordable inland.

resources.title: Banking — Los Angeles
resources.body: Opening a US bank account typically requires an in-person visit with ID and a US taxpayer identification number. Newcomers can often open with a passport plus SSN or ITIN and proof of local address.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — Los Angeles
resources.body: Public schools are run by the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD), the second-largest US district; enrollment is address-based. Numerous private and international schools offer IB and other curricula.

resources.title: Registration & admin — Los Angeles
resources.body: The US has no local residence-registration system. Foreign nationals' status is governed by their visa; immigration matters are handled federally by USCIS. New residents update their address with USCIS (AR-11) and other agencies.

resources.title: Tax & finance — Los Angeles
resources.body: Residents file federal taxes with the IRS and state taxes with California's Franchise Tax Board. Workers need a Social Security Number (SSN); those ineligible use an ITIN. California has state income tax in addition to federal.

resources.title: Transport — Los Angeles
resources.body: Los Angeles is car-centric but has a growing public transit network run by LA Metro (buses and rail) using the TAP card. Foreign driving licences generally cannot be directly exchanged; residents must obtain a California licence via the DMV. There is no universal public healthcare registration.

resources.title: Housing — New York
resources.body: New York City has an extremely competitive and expensive rental market, especially in Manhattan. Leases usually require proof of income (often 40x monthly rent), credit check, and sometimes a guarantor for newcomers without US credit history.

resources.title: Banking — New York
resources.body: Opening a US bank account typically requires a Social Security Number (SSN) or ITIN, a passport, and proof of a US address. Major national banks have extensive branch networks across NYC.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — New York
resources.body: New York City operates the largest public school system in the US via the NYC Department of Education, alongside numerous private and international schools offering IB and other curricula.

resources.title: Registration & admin — New York
resources.body: The US has no local residence registration system. New arrivals enter on a visa with an I-94 admission record and must apply for a Social Security Number if authorized to work.

resources.title: Tax & finance — New York
resources.body: US federal income tax is administered by the IRS. Residents need a Social Security Number (SSN) or, if ineligible, an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) to file. New York State and New York City also levy income taxes.

resources.title: Transport — New York
resources.body: New York City's public transit is run by the MTA, including the 24-hour subway and extensive bus network. Fares use the OMNY contactless system or MetroCard. Newcomers may exchange or apply for a driver's license through the NY DMV. There is no universal public healthcare registration; coverage is via employer or private insurance.

resources.title: Housing — San Francisco
resources.body: San Francisco is one of the most expensive US rental markets. One-bedroom apartments in central neighborhoods typically run around $3,000/month. Landlords usually require first month plus a security deposit (legally capped, commonly one month's rent), proof of income (often 2-3x rent), credit check, and references. Rent-controlled units exist for many older buildings.

resources.title: Banking — San Francisco
resources.body: Opening a US bank account in San Francisco typically requires a government-issued photo ID (passport), a Social Security Number (SSN) or ITIN, and proof of US address. Newcomers without an SSN can sometimes open accounts with a passport and ITIN. Major national banks operate extensive branch networks in the city.

resources.title: Schools & childcare — San Francisco
resources.body: Public schools are run by the San Francisco Unified School District (SFUSD) and follow the California/Common Core curriculum. The city also has numerous private and international schools offering IB, AP, and other curricula. Public school enrollment uses a district assignment/lottery process rather than strict catchment.

resources.title: Registration & admin — San Francisco
resources.body: The United States has no local residence-registration requirement equivalent to European systems. Key first administrative steps for a foreign worker are securing the correct visa status, obtaining a Social Security Number, and (if driving) a California driver's license. Address is updated with individual agencies (USPS, DMV, IRS) rather than a central registry.

resources.title: Tax & finance — San Francisco
resources.body: US federal income tax is administered by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS); California state income tax is administered by the Franchise Tax Board. Workers need an SSN (or ITIN if ineligible for an SSN) to be paid and to file returns. San Francisco residents are subject to federal, California state, and certain local taxes.

resources.title: Transport — San Francisco
resources.body: Public transit is operated by the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), branded Muni, covering buses, light rail, historic streetcars, and cable cars. Regional rail/BART connects to the wider Bay Area. Fares use the regional Clipper card. A foreign driver must obtain a California driver's license (California does not have reciprocal exchange for most countries; a road and knowledge test is generally required). Healthcare is private, insurance-based, with no national registration; coverage is via employer plans or Covered California.
